v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version. Concepts are the catalog's w09 slugs (game-modeling, rules-engines), both already listed in catalog v1.0.119. Title and setting from the Workshop bible v1.0.1 (the catalog's lld title is Chess); w08 has no file yet, so next follows the bible's w10 row. Of the bible's three wrong ideas, check-the-king's-square is what the as-built program already does and store-the-board-more-carefully is the same check again, so the two bad options are a look-back window (the last 10 moves on the tape) and switching castling off for the figure (the bible's ban castling). Every name was chosen after the name lookup and a scan for names inside names (Erconwald, Euphrosyne, Zinovy, Dafydd, Ordgar, Fernihough, and the handle endings gaius and wiglaf); candidates that clashed were dropped before drafting, so no name in this file was renamed.
title: Castling Twice
setting: the workshop's own chess automaton, played by a chess club at night

post.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
post.title: I finish my late great-aunt's machines at night. Her chess automaton castled on Thursday, twenty moves after its king had stepped out and back. The club's arbiter stopped the game.

blocks.text: My great-aunt, Winifrith Torvaine, built coin-operated machines and clockwork figures for sixty years. She died in the spring and left me her workshop. I'm Odgerel. I program on night shifts and finish her machines in the evenings. Each has a paper work order tied on with string.

The oldest is her chess automaton: a machine that plays by itself, built as a seated figure at a real chessboard. A small switch under each square feels whether a piece stands there. A little computer inside picks the figure's moves, and its arm makes them. It always plays Black.

blocks.title: WORK ORDER 7. Fernihough Chess Club, Thursday nights from 10 September.
items: The figure plays one member at a time, from 21:30.
Finish the rules program. The figure must never make an illegal move.
If a member makes an illegal move, light the red lamp and wait.
Print every move on the paper tape.

blocks.text: Winifrith wrote the program as classes. A class is a pattern for one kind of thing in code, like a blank form; each thing made from it is an object.

What an object keeps track of is called its state. The Game object's state is the board, whose turn it is, and the list of moves so far, which it prints on the tape. A Rules object answers one question: is this move legal, allowed by the Laws of Chess, the official rule book? Each turn the figure asks it about every move it could make, then picks one. Each member's move is checked the same way.

One rule was left for me to finish: castling. Once a game, a player may move the king two squares towards one of its rooks, the corner pieces. Then that rook jumps to the square the king passed over. It counts as one move, and tucks the king away in a corner.

Squares are named by column letter and row number; Black's king starts on e8. A king is in check when an enemy piece could take it on the next move. Here is my castling check. Each line is one test, and castling is legal only if all pass:

Rules.canCastle(board, colour, side)
  king on its start square       e8
  rook on its start square       h8
  squares between them empty     f8 g8
  king not in check; crosses and lands on no attacked square

On Thursday 8 October the figure played Euphrosyne. Erconwald, the club's arbiter, the referee who settles questions about the rules, wrote every move on a scoresheet. Here are three lines of the figure's tape: time, move number, Euphrosyne's move as White, then the figure's reply as Black:

21:51:40   9  bishop c4-b5, check   king e8-f8
21:56:02  11  pawn a2-a3            king f8-e8
22:47:13  31  pawn h2-h3            castles: king e8-g8, rook h8-f8

Erconwald stopped the game at once, pointed at move 9 on the scoresheet, and read me the Laws: the right to castle is lost if the king has already moved. Stepping back to e8 doesn't give it back. Euphrosyne and Dafydd agreed to call the game off.
The board showed a king that had never moved. The scoresheet remembered that it had.
The king came back to e8 at move 11, twenty moves before it castled. In the four Thursdays before, the figure's king had never moved before it castled, and no member had castled after moving theirs.
Beside the program, Winifrith's notebook has one line in pencil: *A dial shows where the hands are, not where they have been.* The club comes back next Thursday. What should I change?

blocks.label: tape_2247_redrawn.png

diagram.aria: Timeline from 21:45:00 to 22:50:00 on Thursday 8 October. The black king stands on e8 until 21:51:40, on f8 until 21:56:02, then on e8 again until 22:47:13. The rook stands on h8 until 22:47:13. canCastle's board tests can pass before 21:51:40, and again from 21:56:02, now wrongly. Under the Laws the right to castle holds until 21:51:40 and is lost from then on. The figure castles at 22:47:13.

blocks.caption: I redrew the game from the tape, from 21:45:00, when f8 and g8 were already empty. The black king left e8 at 21:51:40, move 9, and was back at 21:56:02, move 11. From then on the board looked as it had before move 9, so canCastle's tests could pass again, marked wrong. Under the Laws, the right to castle had gone at move 9, shown as the gap. At 22:47:13 the figure castled.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Run your four tests at 22:47:13, one by one, against the board as it stood. Each one passed. Now look at what canCastle is handed: the board, a colour and a side, nothing about the past. Is there anything on a board that tells a king that moved at move 9 from one that never moved? Then read the Laws' castling rule again, word by word, and write down what it asks about. Where in your program does that answer live today? And castling may not be the only rule that cares about what happened earlier, not just where the pieces stand. Read the pawn rules too.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: The Game object has the whole list of moves; it just never hands it to Rules. Each turn the figure asks Rules about every move it could make, about 30 moves in the middle of a game. To replay a move is to make it again on a spare board in memory. Winifrith's little computer takes about 5 ms, five thousandths of a second, to replay one.

comments.author: u/last_ten_moves_gaius
comments.text: You already print every move. Before castling, read back the last 10 moves on the tape for a king or rook move by that side. A king that wanders off and comes home does it within a couple of moves, so ten is plenty, and it's 10 lines of tape instead of the whole game. Simple, fast, done by Thursday.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: Dafydd would rather switch castling off for the figure altogether. Dafydd says it beats most of the club without castling, and a move it never makes can't be illegal.

comments.author: u/replay_from_one_wiglaf
comments.text: Don't keep anything extra that can drift out of step with the game. The move list is the truth. Every time Rules is asked about a move, replay the game from move 1 and look at what has moved. It's always right, and there's nothing new to keep correct.

reply.prompt: The club comes back next Thursday. What should Odgerel change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Store each right to castle in the Game's state, and clear it when its king or rook moves.
options.part2: I gave the Game object four rights to castle, one per rook, all held at the start of a game, and made every move go through one method, Game.apply. A king move clears both of its side's rights; a rook leaving its corner, or taken there, clears that rook's right. canCastle now asks the state for the right, and keeps its board tests for the squares between and for check. On the bench, Thursday's game: move 9 clears Black's two rights, move 11 gives nothing back, and at move 31 castling is not on the figure's list, so it plays another move. On Thursday 22 October the figure castled at move 7, legally, and Black's rights cleared. Zinovy's king stepped out at move 4 and back at move 5, and at move 38 Zinovy tried to castle. The red lamp lit, and Erconwald had the move taken back. The new duty showed in December: Dafydd asked to finish an unfinished game from Erconwald's written position, and I had to type in the four rights by hand, as well as setting out the pieces.
options.senior: Castling depends on the past, so the past has to be recorded somewhere the rule can read it. Keep the small fact the rule needs, a right per rook, in the game's state, and change it in one place, the method every move goes through. Then the check costs nothing extra at move 31 or move 300, and a king that steps out and back can't fool it. The price is discipline: every way a position can change, including take-backs and positions typed in by hand, has to keep the state right.

options.text: Before castling, read back the last 10 moves on the tape for a king or rook move by that side.
options.verdict: A window too short for history
options.part2: I added the search and replayed Thursday's game on the bench. At move 31 it read back moves 21 to 30, found no king or rook move, and the figure castled again: moves 9 and 11 were too far back. I made it 30 moves, and the bench game came out right. On Thursday 22 October Zinovy's king stepped out at move 4, after a check from the figure's bishop, and back at move 5. At move 38 Zinovy castled. The search read back moves 8 to 37, found nothing, and the figure accepted the castle and replied. Erconwald caught it on the scoresheet and stopped the game, and Dafydd called it off: the second game in three Thursdays spoiled by my program.
options.senior: A look-back window guesses how far back the past can matter, and the Laws don't put a limit on it: a king that moved at move 4 has lost the right at move 400. Any window short enough to be cheap misses a long game, and a window as long as the game is just a slow replay. Remember the fact when it happens instead of searching for it later.

options.text: Each time Rules is asked about a move, replay the whole game from move 1 and see what has moved.
options.part2: I made Rules replay the game from move 1, on a spare board, for every question. On the bench, Thursday's game: at move 31 the replay finds the king's step at move 9, and castling is refused. On Thursday 22 October the figure castled legally at move 7, and Zinovy's castle at move 38 lit the red lamp. Nothing illegal got through. But every question now replays every single move before it, by either side. With 30 questions a turn, as the bench counts them, and 5 ms a single move: at move 31 each question replays 61 single moves, 9,150 ms a turn; at move 60, 17,850 ms. Each player has 60 minutes on the chess clock, which counts down only while it is that player's turn. Over a 60-move game, the replays alone would take 9 minutes of the figure's 60. Members have started tapping the table while the figure sits still.
options.senior: Replaying is always right because it reads the truth, the move list, every time. But the work for one question grows with the length of the game, and the work for a whole game grows with the square of its length. It is a fine way to check a design, or to rebuild state after a crash. As the everyday path, it pays again and again for a fact that could have been written down once, when the king moved.

options.text: Switch castling off for the figure, as Dafydd wants: a move it never makes can never be illegal.
options.part2: I switched castling off for the figure. On the bench, Thursday's game reaches move 31 and the figure plays another move. On Thursday 22 October, at move 7, castling was legal for the figure and it could not do it; Erconwald thought its king stood exposed in the middle for the rest of the game. At move 38 Zinovy castled, after the king had stepped out at move 4 and back at move 5. The rules program still judged a member's castling by the board alone, so the figure accepted it and replied. Erconwald caught it on the scoresheet and stopped the game, and Dafydd called it off.
options.senior: Removing a feature hides one symptom and leaves the cause: the program still can't know whether a king has moved, and the same check judges the opponent's moves. It also makes the figure play worse than the Laws allow. When a rule depends on history, the model has to hold that history; turning the rule off for one side doesn't make the other side's answers true.

sim.title: Run Thursday's game through the rules program
sim.lede: You're Odgerel at the workbench, replaying a game from 21:30:00, before its first move. The sim holds only the moves that touch a king or castling. Thursday 8 October, Euphrosyne against the figure: the black king e8-f8 at move 9 (21:51:40), back f8-e8 at move 11 (21:56:02), and the figure's castling question at move 31 (22:47:13). Thursday 22 October, Zinovy against the figure: the white king e1-f1 at move 4 (21:36:10), back at move 5 (21:37:45), the figure's castling question at move 7 (21:41:20) and Zinovy's castle at move 38 (22:58:30). At every castling question the rook is in its corner, the squares between are empty and nothing is attacked, so the board tests pass whenever the king stands on its start square. Moves are numbered in pairs, White then Black: before White's move n come 2n - 2 single moves, before Black's 2n - 1. Replaying takes 5 ms a single move; the figure asks 30 questions a turn, and a member's move is 1 question. Pick a game and a design.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Step once and watch the black king leave e8. Play the rest: canCastle says yes at move 31. Try reading back the last 10 moves, then the last 30, then switch the game to 22 October. Switch castling off and count the legal castle refused at move 7. Replay from move 1 and read the time that turn took. Last, keep the rights in the game's state, in both games.

explain.oneLine: Nothing on the board was wrong. canCastle judged castling from where the pieces stood, but the Laws make it depend on whether the king or rook has ever moved, a fact only the game's history holds, so a king that had stepped out and back looked new.

steps.title: What canCastle saw at 22:47:13.
steps.text: First, the figure asked Rules whether it could castle king side. Second, canCastle looked at e8 and found the black king: pass. Third, it looked at h8 and found the rook: pass. Fourth, it found f8 and g8 empty: pass. Fifth, the king was not in check, and neither f8 nor g8 was under attack: pass. All four tests passed, so castling went on the figure's list, it chose castling, and the arm made it. The Laws ask one more thing, which no test asked: has this king, or this rook, ever moved? The answer was yes, at move 9, and nothing canCastle was handed could say so, because it was handed the board, a colour and a side, and nothing about the past.

steps.title: Why never before, and why move 31.
steps.text: A board shows where the pieces are, not how they got there. Most of the time that is enough: a king that has moved usually stands somewhere else, so the first test fails, and that is why the check held for the four Thursdays before. It goes wrong only when the king steps out and comes back. Euphrosyne's check at move 9 pushed the king to f8, and at move 11 the figure brought it home. From then on the board looked exactly as if the king had never moved. Winifrith's line says why that matters: a dial shows where the hands are, not where they have been. The other tests waited until move 31, when they all passed together.

steps.title: Model the game, not only the board.
steps.text: The game's state is everything the rules need to judge the next move, and the board is only part of it. The rest: whose turn it is; four rights to castle, one per rook (White king side, White queen side, Black king side, Black queen side); the en passant square, the square a pawn has just skipped over by moving two squares, which an enemy pawn may capture onto on the very next move only; and the move counts the draw rules use. Chess programs write a position down in FEN, short for Forsyth-Edwards Notation: a one-line record with six fields, and castling and en passant are two of them. If FEN needs a fact to describe a position, so does your Game object.

steps.title: A rules engine: small checks, each reading the state.
steps.text: A rules engine is a set of small rules, each a condition and what follows from it. For chess, each check answers one question about a move by reading the game's state: does this piece move that way; is the path clear; would the move leave its own king in check; for castling, is the right still held; for en passant, does the capture land on the en passant square. First, a move comes in. Second, each check reads the state and says yes or no. Third, the move is legal only if every check says yes. Fourth, Game.apply makes the move and updates the state, in one place. What can go wrong: a check that works out the past for itself, from the board or from the move list, instead of reading the state.

steps.title: The fix, step by step.
steps.text: First, add four rights to castle to the Game's state, all held at the start of a game. Second, route every move through Game.apply: a king move, castling included, clears both of its side's rights; a rook leaving a1, h1, a8 or h8 clears that rook's right; a capture on one of those squares clears the right of the rook taken there. Third, change canCastle to ask the state whether the right is held, and keep its board tests for the squares between and for check. Fourth, treat en passant the same way: Game.apply sets the en passant square after a two-square pawn move and clears it after any other move. What can go wrong: a take-back, or a position typed in from a scoresheet, must set the state too, rights included.

diagram.aria: The fix. Every move goes through Game.apply, which updates the Game's state: the board, whose turn, four rights to castle and the en passant square. After move 9 Black's rights are gone. Rules reads the state, and its four checks each answer one question: the piece moves that way, the path is clear, the king is safe, the right to castle is held.

nodes.label: Rules
nodes.sub: legal if every check says yes

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for next Thursday. Every move goes through Game.apply, the one place that changes the Game's state: the board, whose turn, four rights to castle and the en passant square. Move 9 takes away Black's two rights, and move 11 gives nothing back. Rules runs its small checks against that state, and the castling check reads the right instead of the board, so at move 31 castling is not on the figure's list.

fix.title: The fix: rights to castle in the Game's state, changed by every move
fix.text: Give the Game object four rights to castle, one per rook, all held at the start. Make Game.apply the only way a move changes the game, and have it clear the rights a move ends: both of a side's rights when its king moves, castling included, and one right when its rook leaves its corner or is taken there. Change canCastle to read the right from the state, keeping its board tests for the squares between and for check. Do the same for en passant with an en passant square in the state, and make take-backs and typed-in positions set the whole state.

limits: The state is only right if every move goes through Game.apply. A move made around it, by a test, a repair tool or a correction typed in by hand, leaves the rights stale, so make apply the only way in.

Take-backs and set-up positions need the whole state. Undoing a move must restore the rights it cleared, so save the state with each move; a game set out from a written position needs its rights and en passant square typed in too.

Some rules need more than the state. FEN, which records the state, still cannot tell whether a draw by threefold repetition may be claimed; for that rule the game must also keep a list of earlier positions.

explain.seniorTake: A board is a snapshot; a game is a history. Before you write a rule, ask what it needs to know, and whether the current picture can show it. When a rule depends on the past (has this piece ever moved, what was the last move, has this position happened before), don't make the rule dig through the past every time, and don't hope the picture will tell you. Decide which facts the state must carry, give them one place where every change goes through, and let each small check read them. FEN is a good test of a chess model: if your Game object can't write one, it is missing state. The habit pays far beyond games: a once-only discount, a first sign-in or a password that may not be reused all need a fact recorded when it happens.

realWorld.title: FIDE Laws of Chess: what castling is
realWorld.text: The FIDE Laws of Chess, taking effect from 1 January 2023, describe castling as "a move of the king and either rook of the same colour along the player’s first rank". The rest of the article says it counts as one move of the king: the king goes two squares towards the rook, and the rook moves to the square the king has just crossed.

realWorld.title: FIDE: the right to castle is lost
realWorld.text: Article 3.8.2.1 reads "The right to castle has been lost:", then "If the king has already moved, or" and "With a rook that has already moved." The article says nothing about getting the right back. Article 3.8.2.2 lists what only prevents castling for now, such as "any piece between the king and the rook with which castling is to be effected."

realWorld.title: FIDE: en passant, on one move only
realWorld.text: Article 3.7.3 lets a pawn capture an opponent's pawn "which has just advanced two squares in one move from its original square" "as though the latter had been moved only one square." And: "This capture is only legal on the move following this advance".

realWorld.title: FEN: the state in one line
realWorld.text: Wikipedia's article on Forsyth-Edwards Notation says "A FEN record contains six fields, each separated by a space." One field gives which castling is still available, as letters for each side and each wing; another is the en passant target square, "a square over which a pawn has just passed while moving two squares".

realWorld.title: FEN's limit: repetition
realWorld.text: The same article: "FEN does not provide sufficient information to decide whether a draw by threefold repetition may be legally claimed". A rule about earlier positions needs a record of earlier positions.

realWorld.title: Martin Fowler, 2009: rules engines
realWorld.text: Fowler describes a rules engine as "a set of production rules, each of which has a condition and an action", and says "simplistically you can think of it as a bunch of if-then statements." He warns that chaining rules "can easily end up being very hard to reason about and debug", and advises to "limit the number of rules by keeping the rules within a narrow context."

asked: How would you model a chess game's state so the rules can be checked?
How would you structure the rules that decide whether a move is legal?
interview.answer: Start with the objects and what each owns. A Board holds the 64 squares and the pieces on them. A Piece knows its colour and kind. A Move says from where, to where, and anything special, such as a promotion. A Game owns the state: the board, whose turn it is, four rights to castle, the en passant square, the counters for the draw rules, and the list of moves, plus a list of earlier positions if you need repetition. One method, apply(move), is the only way the state changes, and it updates every field: a king move clears both of that side's rights, a rook leaving or being taken on its corner clears one, a two-square pawn move sets the en passant square and any other move clears it. Then the rules: a set of small checks, each answering one question by reading the state, such as does this piece move that way, is the path clear, would my own king be left in check, is the castling right held, does this capture land on the en passant square. A move is legal if every check passes; the legal-move list is every candidate that passes. Keep each check narrow and independent, so a new rule is a new check. Name the trap: anything that depends on the past, castling and en passant above all, cannot be judged from the board alone, and replaying the game for every question is right but costs more every move. A good self-test is FEN: if your Game can't write it, it is missing state.

terms.def: The workshop Winifrith Torvaine left to Odgerel: half-finished coin-operated machines and clockwork figures, each with a paper work order tied on and a program to match.
A machine that works when you put a coin in, such as a ticket machine.
A paper slip saying what a client wants made or finished. Work order 7 is the Fernihough Chess Club's: finish the automaton's rules program, signed by Dafydd.
A machine that plays chess by itself. Winifrith's is a seated clockwork figure at a real chessboard, with a switch under each square, a little computer inside and an arm that moves its pieces.
What Odgerel calls the chess automaton. It always plays Black.
The club in this story. Dafydd is its secretary and Erconwald its arbiter; Euphrosyne, Zinovy and Ordgar are members who play the figure on Thursday nights.
The referee at a chess game, who settles questions about the rules and can stop a game. Erconwald is the club's.
A written list of every move in a game, kept by hand. Erconwald's showed the king's step at move 9.
The strip the figure prints every move on: the time, the move number, White's move and Black's reply.
The lamp on the figure that the work order says to light when a member makes an illegal move. The figure then waits.
Each square is named by its column letter, a to h, and its row number, 1 to 8. White's king starts on e1 and Black's on e8; the rooks start in the corners.
Chess pieces. The king must not be captured; the queen is the strongest piece; rooks start in the corners; a bishop moves diagonally; a pawn moves straight ahead, one square, or two from its start.
When a pawn reaches the far row it becomes another piece, usually a queen. A move that promotes has to say which piece.
A king is in check when an enemy piece could take it on the next move. A player must get out of check at once.
Once a game, the king moves two squares towards one of its rooks, and that rook jumps to the square the king passed over. It counts as one move, and tucks the king into a corner.
The two wings of the board. Castling king side uses the rook on h1 or h8; queen side, the rook on a1 or a8.
Each rook gives its side a right to castle with it. The Laws say the right is lost for good once the king has moved, or that rook has; stepping back doesn't give it back.
The official rules of chess, published by FIDE, the international chess federation. The version used here took effect on 1 January 2023.
A move the Laws of Chess allow in this position. An illegal move is one they don't.
The list of steps a computer follows. Winifrith wrote hers in the same notebooks as her clockwork.
A pattern for one kind of thing in code, like a blank form (s5e04). Game and Rules are classes.
One real thing made from a class, like one filled-in form (s5e04). Each game played is a Game object.
What an object keeps track of. The Game object's state, as built: the board, whose turn it is and the list of moves so far.
A set of steps a class can carry out, such as canCastle() or apply().
Winifrith's class for one game of chess. It holds the board, whose turn it is and the move list, and prints each move on the tape.
Winifrith's class that answers one question: is this move legal? The figure asks it about every move it could make, and about each member's move.
The castling check Odgerel finished: four tests on the board (king and rook on their start squares, the squares between empty, no check or attacked square). It is handed only the board.
To make a game's moves again, one by one, on a spare board in memory. Winifrith's little computer takes about 5 ms a single move.
One move by one side. Moves are numbered in pairs, White then Black, so before Black's 31st move come 61 single moves.
Short for millisecond, a thousandth of a second. 5 ms is five thousandths of a second.
Two clocks side by side, one per player; only the clock of the player whose turn it is counts down. In the club's games each player has 60 minutes.
Reading back only the last few moves, such as the last 10 lines of the tape, to look for something in the past. Anything further back is missed.
Everything the rules need to judge the next move: the board, whose turn it is, four rights to castle, the en passant square and the counts the draw rules use.
In the fix, the one method every move goes through. It makes the move and updates the state, for example clearing the rights to castle a king or rook move ends.
A set of small rules, each a condition and what follows from it, run against some data. Here, small checks that each read the game's state and say yes or no to a move.
A rule written as a condition and an action: if this is true, do that. Martin Fowler describes a rules engine as a set of them.
One rule's action making another rule's condition true, so rules set each other off. Fowler warns it gets hard to follow.
When a pawn moves two squares from its start, an enemy pawn beside where it lands may take it as if it had moved one. Only on the very next move.
The square a pawn has just skipped over by moving two squares. It is part of the game's state, set by that move and cleared by the next.
A standard one-line record of a chess position with six fields: the pieces, whose turn, castling still available, the en passant square and two move counts.
A draw is a game that ends with no winner. One way is threefold repetition: the same position three times, which a player may claim. FEN can't show it.
A picture of how things stand at one moment, with nothing about how they got there. A chessboard is one.
Undoing a move, as when the arbiter has an illegal move taken back. The state must go back to what it was too.
A yes-or-no value a program keeps, such as whether a customer has used a first-order discount.
Grows like the length times itself: twice as long a game means about four times the total work. Replaying for every question grows this way.
Odgerel's workbench: the sim, which replays a game's king moves and castling questions through whichever design you pick.
How many moves the figure asks Rules about each turn. The bench counts 30; a member's move is 1 question.

atWork: Look for once-only rules judged from a snapshot. Common ones: a first-order discount given when a customer has no orders in the table, where cancelled orders are deleted; a free trial offered when an account has no subscription now, though it had one last year; "you may not reuse your last 5 passwords" checked against a list that a reset clears. Each is a king back on e8: the current data looks new, while the history says the right was used. Read-only access to the code and the data is enough. Search for checks of the form "count is zero" or "no record exists" that grant something once, then ask what deletes those records. Fix it the way the Game's rights work: record the fact when it happens, in one place every path goes through, and have the check read that fact.

recall.prompt: A food delivery app gives 20% off a customer's first order. At checkout it looks in the orders table: no orders for this customer, so the discount applies. Cancelled orders are deleted from that table. On a busy weekend, support finds customers who placed and cancelled an order getting the discount again, some of them several times. What is wrong with the design, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The rule is about history (has this customer ever ordered?), but the check reads only what is in the table now, and a delete makes the customer look new
Record the fact when it happens: a flag kept on the customer, set once and never cleared by a cancel
Every path that places an order goes through one method that sets it, and the discount check reads it

recall.model: The rule is about history: has this customer ever ordered? But the check reads only what is in the orders table now, and a cancel deletes the order, so the customer looks new again, like the king back on e8. Record the fact when it happens: a first-order-used flag on the customer, set once when the discount is used and never cleared by a cancel. Make every path that places an order go through one method that sets it, so no checkout can skip it, and have the discount check read the flag instead of counting orders.

recall.prompt: Which of these can a rules program decide correctly from the board alone, with nothing else in the game's state?
options: Whether Black may castle king side
Whether a white pawn on e2 may move two squares to e4
Whether a pawn may capture en passant
Whether a king that left e8 and came back may castle
recall.why: A pawn still on its start row may move two squares if both squares ahead are empty, and the board shows all of that. Castling depends on whether the king or rook has ever moved, and en passant on what the last move was: history a board can't show.

recall.prompt: A teammate proposes that the rules program never stores anything about the past: for every question about a move, it replays the game from move 1 on a spare board. The figure asks 30 questions a turn, and replaying one single move takes 5 ms. What does this cost as games get longer, and what would you do instead?

keyIdeas.idea: Each question's cost grows with the length of the game: it replays every single move before it
Over a whole game, the total grows with the square of its length
Keep the needed facts, such as the rights to castle, in the game's state, changed once per move by one method

recall.model: It is always right, but it costs more every move. Each question replays every single move before it, so its cost grows with the length of the game: at Black's 31st move, 30 questions times 61 single moves times 5 ms is 9,150 ms; at move 60, 17,850 ms. Over a whole game the total grows with the square of its length: 9 minutes for a 60-move game. Instead, keep the facts the rules need, the four rights to castle and the en passant square, in the game's state, and change them once per move in one method, Game.apply. Each question then reads the state at no extra cost.

recall.prompt: At Black's 31st move, how many single moves, by either side, has the game had before it?
recall.why: Moves are numbered in pairs, White then Black. Before Black's 31st move come 30 full pairs, 60 single moves, plus White's 31st: 61. A full replay reads all 61.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The rights to castle live in the Game object now, and the figure hasn't castled wrongly since. I left Winifrith's en passant check as she wrote it: my pawn on its fifth row counting from its own side, an enemy pawn right beside it, and the square behind that enemy pawn empty. On Thursday 7 January at 22:12, at move 16, the figure's pawn on e4 took Ordgar's pawn on d4 that way, landing on d3. Ordgar's pawn had moved d2-d4, two squares at once, at move 14. Every test in the check passed. Erconwald stopped the game and said the capture came two moves too late.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why was the capture illegal when every test passed, and how should the program judge en passant?

keyIdeas.idea: En passant is only legal on the move straight after the two-square advance: a fact about history
Keep an en passant square in the game's state: set by a two-square pawn move, cleared by the next move, read by the check
It is the castling mistake again: a rule about the past judged from the board alone

coldCase.model: It's the castling mistake again, in a smaller place. Ordgar's pawn moved d2-d4 at move 14, two squares at once, and the Laws let a pawn beside it take it as if it had moved one, but only on the move straight after. The figure took it at move 16. Every test in Winifrith's check passed because each one reads the board alone, and a pawn that arrived two moves ago looks exactly like one that arrived just now. Keep an en passant square in the game's state, as the rights to castle are: Game.apply sets it to d3 when a pawn moves d2-d4, and clears it on the next move, whatever that move is. The en passant check then asks only whether the capture lands on that square.
